domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal & pediatric physiology, pediatric airway, congenital conditions, fluid & glucose management, emergence, common procedures)
stem: Why is brief laryngospasm especially dangerous in small children compared with adults?
answer: Children have reduced FRC and high cardiac output; even brief laryngospasm causes rapid hypoxemia.
rationale: Reduced FRC means less oxygen reserve; high metabolic rate consumes oxygen faster, leaving minimal time before dangerous desaturation.

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal & pediatric physiology, pediatric airway, congenital conditions, fluid & glucose management, emergence, common procedures)
stem: What is the treatment sequence for laryngospasm in a child?
answer: 100% O2 via positive pressure facemask + oral/nasal airway + deepen anesthesia IV; refractory: succinylcholine 0.25-0.5 mg/kg + intubation.
rationale: Early positive pressure and anesthetic deepening break most laryngospasm; succinylcholine achieves complete muscle relaxation in refractory cases.

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal & pediatric physiology, pediatric airway, congenital conditions, fluid & glucose management, emergence, common procedures)
stem: What is the primary and most effective treatment for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy?
answer: Adenotonsillectomy; recommended for most pediatric patients with AHI >9 events/hour or mild-moderate OSA with significant symptoms.
rationale: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the most common cause of pediatric OSA; surgical removal relieves the obstruction.
confusable_with: CPAP (alternative for adults, not first-line for children with hypertrophy)

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal & pediatric physiology, pediatric airway, congenital conditions, fluid & glucose management, emergence, common procedures)
stem: When can pediatric patients with recent URI undergo brief non-airway ENT procedures?
answer: Practical considerations allow minor ENT surgery (e.g. myringotomy) during URI when surgery will likely decrease infection frequency; risks are manageable.
rationale: URI causes airway hyperreactivity and increases laryngospasm risk but can be managed; postponement for every URI would delay needed procedures indefinitely.

domain: Pediatric anesthesia (neonatal & pediatric physiology, pediatric airway, congenital conditions, fluid & glucose management, emergence, common procedures)
stem: Children with URI have approximately what relative risk of laryngospasm compared with healthy children?
answer: Approximately 3.4 times higher risk of laryngospasm with recent URI (within 1 month).
rationale: Upper airway inflammation from URI increases mucosal sensitivity and reflex laryngospasm; risk persists up to 4-6 weeks after URI.

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: Name three adjunctive therapies that improve oxygenation in severe ARDS but are not without risk.
answer: Inhaled nitric oxide, inhaled prostacyclin (or PGE1), and prone positioning.
rationale: Each improves V/Q matching or recruits dependent alveoli; but NO may cause methemoglobinemia, prone positioning risks pressure injuries.

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: What is the current evidence for corticosteroids in ARDS and specifically in COVID-19 lung disease?
answer: Meta-analysis suggests moderate-dose corticosteroids likely improve morbidity/mortality in ARDS (controversial); steroids are definitively beneficial in COVID-19 lung disease.
rationale: Dexamethasone reduced mortality in RECOVERY trial for COVID-19 requiring oxygen; ARDS steroid data are mixed but lean toward benefit in early/moderate disease.

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: In COVID-19 ARDS, what additional therapy beyond lung-protective ventilation is indicated?
answer: Anticoagulant therapy (increased PE risk in COVID-19) plus prone positioning.
rationale: COVID-19 causes hypercoagulability with high PE rates; prone positioning improves oxygenation in severe COVID ARDS.

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: Management of cardiogenic pulmonary edema targets what physiologic parameter and by what interventions?
answer: Decrease pulmonary capillary pressure (Pc); by improving LV function, correcting fluid overload with diuretics, or reducing pulmonary blood flow.
rationale: Cardiogenic edema results from elevated Pc; reducing LV filling pressures decreases hydrostatic transudation into the alveolus.

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: What FiO2 threshold and duration beyond which is oxygen toxicity a concern?
answer: FiO2 >50-60% for prolonged periods risks pulmonary toxicity; 100% O2 for up to 10-20 hours is generally considered safe.
rationale: Oxygen free radicals damage DNA, proteins, and lipids in alveolar cells; minimizing FiO2 with PEEP recruitment is a core ARDS strategy.
